analysis.one_liner: Caps interest and fees on all consumer loans at 36% a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 111th Congress ended, with only 4 of 58 Democratic senators signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write a 36% annual ceiling on the combined cost of consumer credit — interest plus fees — into federal law for the first time. It targets payday loans, car title loans, bank overdraft fees, tax refund anticipation loans, and credit cards with junk fees, all of which can run far above 36% today. Lenders who broke the cap would face prison and fines, and any loan over 36% could not be enforced in court. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who pay triple-digit annual rates: roughly, in the bill's own findings, $17.5 billion a year on high-cost overdraft loans, up to $8.6 billion on payday loans, and nearly $900 million on tax refund anticipation loans [S3]. Credit card holders charged high rates plus late, over-limit, and cash-advance fees would also be covered, since the cap counts all those fees together [S3]. State attorneys general could sue on borrowers' behalf [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Bars any creditor from extending consumer credit where combined interest and fees exceed 36% a year, counting late fees, over-limit fees, overdraft fees, cash-advance fees, credit insurance, and ancillary products in the total so the cap can't be evaded with add-on charges [S3].

Nullifies loans made in violation of the cap: any payment on such a loan is unenforceable and the lender must return principal, interest, and fees, and violations carry up to 1 year in prison and a fine of the greater of triple the accrued debt or $50,000 [S3].
Lets state attorneys general enforce the cap in federal court within 3 years of a violation [S2].
Replaces APR disclosures with a single 'FAIR' (fee and interest rate) figure on credit card statements whenever the finance charge exceeds 50 cents per billing cycle [S2].
Leaves stricter state usury laws fully in place and explicitly does not preempt them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Payday, car title, and tax refund anticipation lenders, whose business model depends on annual rates of 300%–400% [S3], and banks and credit card issuers that collect overdraft, late, and over-limit fees — the bill's findings total these charges at roughly $27 billion a year [S3]. Small lenders would lose the ability to price for risk through fees.

drawbacks.text: A hard 36% cap could make small, short-term loans unprofitable for licensed lenders to make at all, leaving some marginal borrowers — those banks and payday lenders say justify higher rates — without access to legal credit or pushing them to unlicensed lenders. The bill acknowledges the concern by encouraging alternatives like installment loans with minimal fees [S3].

The penalty of voiding the loan and forcing repayment of all principal, interest, and fees applies to any violation, which would expose legitimate lenders that miscount a fee to large liabilities and could make some lenders exit consumer lending rather than risk it [S3].

Counting every fee (late fees, overdraft fees, cash-advance fees) into one 36% number is stricter than the 2006 military lending cap, which covered a narrower set of products, so lenders would face a harder compliance line across all consumer credit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and concrete: borrowers currently pay roughly $27 billion a year in overdraft, payday, and refund-advance charges at rates the bill's findings put at 300% to 3,500% annualized [S3]. The main cost is real but narrower: some borrowers who use payday loans today might lose access to that credit, because lenders say they cannot profitably lend small amounts at 36%. A well-designed cap with a transition to installment products would address that; this bill encourages such alternatives but does not require them. On balance, the bill transfers costs from heavily indebted households to high-cost lenders.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on February 26, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S5].
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded after the referral [S5].

The bill's own findings set the scale of what it targeted: consumers pay about $17.5 billion a year in high-cost overdraft loans, up to $8.6 billion in payday loans, and nearly $900 million in tax refund anticipation loans [S3].
A federal 36% cap already applied to loans made to service members and their families under a 2006 law, and the bill would have extended that standard to all consumers [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, banks, and credit card issuers are better off because the bill died: they kept collecting overdraft, late, and triple-digit-rate charges that the bill would have capped and, in violation cases, clawed back. Borrowers paying those costs saw no change.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to establish a national 36% usury cap and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the two years before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill sat in, never scheduled action on it.

against.name: Payday lending and bank fee industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed a national 36% rate cap on consumer credit, which would eliminate the fee and interest revenue the bill's findings total at roughly $27 billion a year.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no split is on the record; the only 5 senators on record — Durbin and 4 cosponsors — were all Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill.

industries.industry: Payday, car title, and tax refund anticipation lenders
industries.note: Their business model is charging 300%–400% annualized rates on small loans; a 36% all-in cap with voidable loans and criminal penalties would shut the model down. The bill's findings show borrowers paying up to $8.6 billion a year to these lenders [S3].

They would lose overdraft, late, over-limit, and cash-advance fee income, which the cap counts into the 36% total; the bill's findings put high-cost overdraft loans alone at $17.5 billion a year [S3].

industries.industry: Credit insurers and sellers of ancillary credit products
industries.note: Credit insurance premiums and add-on products would count toward the 36% cap, reducing what lenders could charge for them and how much of them could be sold [S3].
